newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish bond yields jump on politics, inflation.
newsitem.headline: Turkish bond yields jump on politics, inflation.

text.p: Turkey's rising political tension and higher-than-expected inflation figures pushed bond yields higher on Tuesday, bankers said.
Bond yields rose seven to 10 points to 103 to 107 percent, and bankers said rates could rise further if uncertainties over the government's fate continue.

"The market thought the rise would end at the 100-percent level in the morning, but the upward trend continued during the day due to increased concerns over the government after the National Security Council's warning on Friday," a private bank treasurer said.
At a meeting on Friday, the military-dominated council ordered Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan to reverse a recent wave of Islamist zeal partly encouraged by his Welfare Party.
On Tuesday, parliament began debating a censure motion from the leading opposition party against Erbakan's government.
"The rates will go up if the government cannot ease the tension in the coming days," the banker said.
In the most active December 1997 paper, the yield jumped seven points from Monday's close to 103.30 percent. The paper's yield with Wednesday value surged to 108.22 percent.
More pressure came when the State Institute of Statistics said February wholesale prices rose 6.2 percent and consumer prices gained 5.7 percent to exceed expectations of up 4.5 to 5.5 percent.
Year-on-year, wholesale prices rose 78.6 percent and consumer prices jumped 77.7 percent.
Inflation and political woes also hampered the treasury's sale of two-year inflation-indexed bonds.
The treasury only sold 18.4 trillion lira ($148.9 million) of consumer price inflation-indexed bonds, which included a risk premium of 25 percent. Total demand was 36.8 trillion lira.

"The timing of the first inflation-indexed bond auction was not good. Political uneasiness, higher-than-expected inflation data, falling stocks, rising bond yields lowered demand for the auction," said a private bank treasurer.
Despite low participation, government officials said the auction result was satisfactory.
"Despite higher-than-expected inflation and negative political developments, there was a enough demand for the auction," State Minister Ufuk Soylemez told Reuters.
He said total after-tax cost of papers to the Treasury was 105 percent, which he said was lower than current bond rates.
"If the inflation falls in coming months, our borrowing cost will be lower," said Soylemez, who oversees the Treasury and privatisation.
Central bank governor Gazi Ercel said on Monday demand for the new inflation-indexed bonds would increase if the tax is charged only on the real return part of bond yields.
Treasury officials said this would require a change in legislation, and there were some studies aimed at changing the taxation of papers.
